title: Renting an Apartment in Spanish: Phrases and Vocabulary
seo_title: Renting an Apartment in Spanish: Phrases and Vocabulary
meta_description: Renting an apartment in Spanish: viewing questions, rent, deposits, guarantors, contracts and problems with the landlord, with Mexico and Spain notes.
excerpt: Viewings, deposits, guarantors and contracts: the words that matter when you rent.
body_html:
Renting an apartment in Spanish involves more specialized vocabulary than most everyday situations, and the stakes are higher: you are agreeing to pay money and sign a contract. The process is similar in Mexico and Spain, but the words differ. An apartment is a departamento in Mexico and a piso in Spain; rent is la renta in Mexico and el alquiler in Spain. This guide covers the questions to ask at a viewing, the money and contract vocabulary, and how to talk to a landlord when something breaks.

Quick answer
  • Apartment: departamento (Mexico), piso (Spain)
  • Rent: ¿Cuánto es la renta al mes?
  • Costs: depósito, mantenimiento, servicios
  • Contract: contrato de arrendamiento, fiador or aval
{{toc}}

Questions to ask at a viewing

  • ¿Cuánto es la renta al mes? How much is the rent per month?
  • ¿Los servicios están incluidos? Are utilities included?
  • ¿Cuánto es el mantenimiento? How much is the maintenance fee?
  • ¿Cuántos meses de depósito piden? How many months’ deposit do you ask for?
  • ¿Se aceptan mascotas? Are pets allowed?
  • ¿Tiene estacionamiento? Does it have parking?
  • ¿Hay problemas de agua o de luz? Are there any problems with water or electricity?
  • ¿Cuándo estaría disponible? When would it be available?

In many Mexican cities, ask about water pressure and storage: some buildings rely on a tinaco (rooftop water tank) or cisterna (underground tank).

{{image:2}}

Requirements and the contract

Landlords in Mexico often ask for:

  • un mes de depósito and el primer mes de renta one month’s deposit and the first month’s rent
  • comprobante de ingresos proof of income
  • identificación oficial official ID
  • un fiador con propiedad a guarantor who owns property in the same city, or a póliza jurídica (rental guarantee insurance) instead

Read the contrato de arrendamiento (lease) carefully. Key phrases to look for: plazo (term, often un año), penalización (penalty for leaving early), incremento anual (yearly increase) and entrega del inmueble (returning the property).

In Mexico, the consumer protection agency Profeco publishes guidance on rental contracts. If the contract is important to you, have it reviewed by someone qualified before signing.

Negotiating

  • ¿La renta es negociable? Is the rent negotiable?
  • ¿Me haría un descuento si firmo por dos años? Would you give me a discount if I sign for two years?
  • ¿Podrían pintar antes de que me mude? Could you paint before I move in?
  • ¿Puedo pagar por transferencia? Can I pay by bank transfer?

Polite, conditional forms like ¿me haría…? and ¿podrían…? make negotiating feel less confrontational. See {{link:polite-requests-in-spanish|polite requests in Spanish}}.

{{book:a-road-in-bloom}}

A sample viewing

Casera: Pásele. Aquí está la sala, y al fondo la cocina.
Come in. Here is the living room, and the kitchen is at the back.

Tú: Está muy bonito. ¿Cuánto es la renta?
It’s very nice. How much is the rent?

Casera: Doce mil al mes, más el mantenimiento, que son ochocientos.
Twelve thousand a month, plus the maintenance fee, which is eight hundred.

Tú: ¿Y el agua y la luz están incluidas?
And are water and electricity included?

Casera: El agua sí, la luz no. Pido un mes de depósito y fiador.
Water is, electricity isn’t. I ask for one month’s deposit and a guarantor.

Tú: Entiendo. ¿Aceptaría una póliza jurídica en lugar de fiador?
I see. Would you accept rental guarantee insurance instead of a guarantor?

When something breaks

  • Hay una fuga de agua en el baño. There’s a water leak in the bathroom.
  • El boiler no prende. The water heater won’t turn on. (Mexico; Spain: el calentador or la caldera)
  • Se fue la luz en el departamento. The power went out in the apartment.
  • ¿Cuándo podría venir alguien a revisarlo? When could someone come to check it?
  • ¿Quién paga la reparación? Who pays for the repair?

Put important requests in writing, even a WhatsApp message: Le escribo para avisarle que… (I’m writing to let you know that…). For more formal messages, see {{link:writing-emails-in-spanish|writing emails in Spanish}}, and for neighbors, {{link:talking-to-neighbors-in-spanish|talking to neighbors in Spanish}}.

{{image:3}}

Common mistakes

  • Apartamento in Mexico. Understood, but departamento is what people say. (Apartamento is common in Colombia and Venezuela.)
  • Depósito in Spain. Spaniards say la fianza.
  • Confusing rentar directions. Rento un departamento can mean you rent it from someone or to someone; context or rento mi departamento a… makes it clear.
  • Los servicios no son incluidos. Use estar for this: Los servicios no están incluidos.
{{quiz}}

Final thoughts

Renting an apartment in Spanish is easier when you know the key words for your country and have your questions ready before the viewing. Ask about every cost, read the contract carefully and put repair requests in writing. For other everyday moments, see {{link:spanish-phrases-for-everyday-situations|Spanish phrases for everyday situations}}.

faq.q: How do you say apartment in Spanish?
faq.a: Departamento in Mexico and Argentina, piso in Spain and apartamento in Colombia and Venezuela.

faq.q: What is a fiador in Mexico?
faq.a: A guarantor, usually someone who owns property in the same city and agrees to cover the rent if the tenant doesn’t pay.

faq.q: What is the difference between renta and alquiler?
faq.a: Both mean rent. Renta is used in Mexico; alquiler is used in Spain and many other countries.

faq.q: What should I check before signing a lease in Spanish?
faq.a: The term (plazo), the deposit, penalties for leaving early, yearly increases and who pays for repairs.
